# GE (GE Aerospace) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Easy to understand at the business-model level: GE Aerospace designs, builds, and services jet engines for commercial and military aircraft, monetized through a low-margin equipment sale followed by decades of high-margin spare-parts and MRO revenue under long-term service agreements. The one genuine complexity is the accounting for those long-term contracts (LTSA revenue recognition, program accounting on engine development costs), which has historically been a source of surprises at this company - a reason to hold management's numbers to a slightly higher standard, not a reason to avoid the business.

## Moat & Durability — Score 8/10
GE Aerospace is one leg of a durable three-way global duopoly/oligopoly (GE/CFM, Rolls-Royce, Pratt & Whitney) protected by regulatory certification costs, decades-long platform life cycles, and sole-source aftermarket parts economics. Airlines cannot swap engines the way they can swap software vendors; once an engine family is certified on an airframe, GE effectively owns that aircraft's engine-parts economics for its operating life. The moat is not absolute - engine choice does happen at the platform-design stage, and next-generation propulsion (open-fan, hybrid-electric) is a multi-decade wildcard - but for the installed base flying today and being delivered over the next decade, the switching costs are about as real as they get in industrials.

## Management & Capital Allocation
The post-2018 turnaround under Larry Culp is a genuine, verifiable story: GE simplified from a sprawling conglomerate into a focused aerospace pure-play via the GE Vernova and GE HealthCare spin-offs, and the FLIGHT DECK lean operating system gives some evidence of operating discipline rather than financial engineering. Debt/equity near 1.1x is moderate, not alarming, for a capital-intensive aerospace manufacturer. But the packet's 48.2% ROE should be read skeptically - it is flattered by a thin equity base (legacy of years of write-downs, pension charges, and buybacks), not purely a signal of exceptional returns on invested capital. What can't be verified from this packet: actual buyback cadence, dividend payout ratio, executive compensation alignment, or capital allocation discipline on the defense/services side of the business.

## Predictability
The aftermarket annuity - spare parts and service on a large, aging installed base - is genuinely predictable revenue once a fleet is flying. But the packet shows 21.1% revenue growth, well above what a mature engine duopoly should sustain organically for long, alongside a null thesis field that gives no color on whether this is a real structural inflection (air-travel recovery, defense budget growth, LEAP ramp finally hitting stride) or a favorable comp. Momentum data reinforces that ambiguity: +33.9% over 12 months, +23.4% over 3 months, RSI14 at 61.7, and price 15.6% above the 200-day moving average - a market that has already extrapolated good news into the price. That combination fails Munger's 'easy decision' test even though the underlying business model is simple.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Execution or share-loss risk on next-gen engines**: LEAP production ramp disappoints, or Rolls-Royce/Pratt & Whitney take incremental share on new platforms, undercutting the growth assumption embedded in a 43x trailing multiple.
2. **Air-travel demand shock**: a recession, fuel-price spike, or geopolitical disruption cuts global flight hours, which directly defers the high-margin aftermarket revenue that is the entire investment thesis - engines sold near breakeven only pay off if planes keep flying.
3. **Priced-for-perfection re-rating**: EV/EBITDA of 34x and an FCF yield of just 1.7% leave essentially no room for a growth disappointment; any stumble triggers a sharp multiple compression, amplified by the balance sheet's moderate leverage.

## Valuation
The packet does not include share price or share count, so per-share figures below rest on an approximate ~1.085B diluted share count (a modeling assumption based on GE Aerospace's known post-spin-off share structure, not sourced from this packet) - this implies a current price near $349/share. Trailing net income backed out from market cap / P/E is roughly $8.8B (~$8.10/share); free cash flow backed out from the FCF yield is roughly $6.6B (~$6.08/share), with the gap versus net income consistent with heavy current reinvestment in LEAP production capacity rather than a red flag on earnings quality.

Treating normalized owner earnings as closer to the ~$8.10/share net-income figure (assuming today's elevated growth capex moderates as the LEAP ramp matures and D&A roughly offsets true maintenance capex over a cycle), and applying a 24x-30x multiple - a premium to the market to reflect the duopoly moat and long-duration aftermarket annuity, but well below the market's current 43x trailing multiple to preserve discipline - yields a fair value range of roughly **$195-$245/share** (midpoint ~$220).

Against an implied current price of ~$349/share, that midpoint implies a margin of safety of **roughly -37%** - the stock is priced meaningfully above what a disciplined owner-earnings approach would pay, even for a business this good.

## The Cloning Caveat
Polen Capital Management, a concentrated quality/growth manager, opened a new GE position sized at 2.22% of portfolio in Q2 2026 - a real, monitored-conviction commitment, though not a top-five bet for a manager who typically runs 20-25 names. Arnold Van Den Berg (Century Management), a deep-value investor, opened a position at just 0.05% of portfolio - functionally a toe-dip, not a statement of conviction from a manager whose sizing usually reflects deep discounts to intrinsic value. Torray Funds' add is 0.03% of portfolio, portfolio dust. Read collectively: a quality-growth manager finds this attractive at current levels, but the value-oriented managers here are barely committing capital - consistent with a good business trading at a price that value discipline says to wait on.

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 4/10.** GE Aerospace is a wonderful, durable-moat business - understandable, oligopolistic, annuity-like once engines are flying - being run by credible management that has genuinely simplified and de-risked the company. But it is priced today for a flawless multi-year ramp: 43x trailing earnings, 34x EV/EBITDA, and a 1.7% FCF yield leave no margin of safety by owner-earnings logic, and the superinvestor buying here is modest, not the kind of concentrated conviction bet that would override valuation discipline. This is a name to keep on the list and revisit on a pullback or a multiple-year growth-into-valuation, not a buy at today's implied price.
momentum_thesis: GE Aerospace's 12-month tape is real and freshly reaccelerated: after round-tripping roughly -6% in the spring (implied by ret_3m of 23.4% exceeding ret_6m of 16.2%), shares ripped higher over the trailing quarter to sit 15.6% above the 200DMA, with RSI14 at 61.7 leaving room before overbought territory kicks in. The 1-month print of just 3.7% shows that sprint cooling off its hot pace — the first crack in an otherwise clean trend structure. Positioning offers no combustible fuel either way: short interest is a token 1.4% of float at 3.6 days to cover, so this isn't a squeeze candidate and there's no smart-money short conviction to fade, while the put-heavy 1.22 OI skew reads more as profit-protection by longs after a big run than genuine bearish positioning. Polen Capital's fresh 2.22%-of-portfolio stake in Q2 is the signal that matters here — a concentrated quality-growth shop putting real size behind a name generating 48% ROE and 21% revenue growth validates the move as fundamentals-led rather than pure chart-chasing, even as Century Management's and Torray's token additions add little conviction weight of their own. The risk sitting underneath all of it is valuation: 43x trailing earnings, 34x EV/EBITDA, and a 1.7% FCF yield leave almost no cushion, and at 1.37 beta this name will amplify any market-wide derating faster than the technicals alone suggest.
